claims.text: The nanoparticles are sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles initially exhibit a metastable FCC structure.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
Heating causes segregation of Au and Cu in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Segregation of Au and Cu is followed by particle loss through evaporation.
Surface-energy-minimization gradients drive Au and Cu segregation and subsequent particle loss.
Surface-energy effects overcome or bypass the sluggish-diffusion barrier in these nanoparticles.
High-index facet exposure and surface-energy gradients lower the activation energy for surface diffusion.
Au and Cu are low-surface-energy elements relative to the other components of this alloy.
Surface-energy minimization rapidly transports Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface enrichment creates a concentration gradient that facilitates Au/Cu evaporation or particle coalescence.
Surface effects dominate over bulk sluggish diffusion in the sub-10 nm size regime.
A critical temperature exists at which Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation rates increase sharply.
The critical temperature depends on whether the initial particle shape is icosahedral or a truncated octahedron.
Enhanced segregation and evaporation widen the nanoparticle size distribution.
Heating drives a shape transition toward spherical particles.
The proposed surface-dominated mechanism is valid only for particles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion dominates and prevents rapid segregation.
Failure of surface-energy-only simulations to reproduce both the experimental critical temperature and Au/Cu enrichment would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The critical activation threshold is initially defined as a specific surface-to-volume geometric limit, but the prediction defines it as a temperature threshold whose value is unknown. Geometry may influence temperature, but the hypothesis does not clearly distinguish these two threshold variables.
